GPUs are a lot more than just "gaming accellerators".
If you do content creation, especially video transcoding, then the Intel Arc cards are the best by a long shot, even the older A series.
They are the only ones which support almost all AV-1 encoding options.
So yes, maybe the Radeon is a better "gaming card", but the Arc cards are better "multi-purpose" GPUs.
I used to be an AMD fan - and I still am for their CPUs - but their GPU encoding capabilities lag behind. And their iGPUs don't even have encoders.... at least Intels iGPUs have video encoders, even AV-1.
People always laugh at Intel's iGPU gaming capabilities, and say that "AMD's iGPUs are much better!"
For gaming, indeed, but for all the rest the Intel iGPUs are way, way better.
When it comes to GPUs, AMD thinks like a "gaming" company, and Intel thinks like a "serious" company. 🙂

text:
Two reasons for game specific tweaks I know of / can think of:
1) apparently game devs actually put out bad / non-standards compliant code shockingly often. So the game driver doesn’t just have to “translate” it, but auto correct some of it.
2) not every game dev is the developers of Doom (modern or OG) and they won’t always use the most performant code, which technically is dependent on what hardware you want to run it on. So if the game developers did something like 2+2+2+2+2+….=200, the driver would probably change that to 2*100 or whatever.

Allegedly, the NVIDIA driver used to improve the multithreading of single threaded graphics APIs, which is why we have more modern APIs that aren’t single threaded. I’ve seen people say that using DXVK (Linux’s DirectX to Vulkan translation layer) can also improve performance in those games even on Windows, because it lets the game multithread that part. Would be interesting to see HardwareUnboxed test that.
